Making best use of railway land
news.body:
The Government has extended KiwiRail’s lease of railway land by 100 years, unlocking the commercial potential of billions of dollars in Crown property, Rail Minister Winston Peters says.

“New Zealanders have invested in their railway estate for generations, and we must make those assets work harder for taxpayers,” Mr Peters says.

“Across the country, valuable railway land sits vacant or underused. We want to turn that wasted potential into productive investment, jobs, and revenue.

“Any smart businessperson knows that the value of land depends on what you can do with it, and how long you have to do it. No developer will invest millions in buildings and infrastructure without certainty they can recover their investment and make a return.

“A short lease limits investment and depresses value. A long lease provides certainty, attracts capital, and unlocks commercial opportunities. That is why we are extending KiwiRail’s lease from 2070 to 2170, putting its landholdings on a near-freehold commercial footing.

“Railway land remains in Crown ownership through the New Zealand Railways Corporation. We are not selling the family silver. We are making it earn its keep.

“We initiated this work in 2018 and were surprised to discover, on returning to the railways portfolio, that it had been left idling by people with no commercial experience.

“Since then officials and KiwiRail have engaged with iwi, whose existing rights of first refusal over railway land remains unchanged, and many have expressed interest in joining investment ventures in railway assets as a result of that engagement.

“Every dollar earned from railway property is a dollar that can be put to work supporting rail rather than coming from taxpayers’ pockets.

“New Zealanders own these valuable assets which were left to rot on the roadside for too long, but with our efforts they will garner a return on them,” Mr Peters says.

news.title: 2026-11-05 - Martin Schlegel: Transmission and conduct of monetary policy in Switzerland
news.body: To achieve its mandate, a central bank needs to understand how its actions affect the financial system and the economy. Switzerland is a small open economy with a stable political and institutional environment. This creates a special setting for monetary policy. Our main tool is the SNB policy rate. If necessary, the SNB also uses other measures. Understanding the transmission of our monetary policy to the Swiss economy is important for the SNB in achieving its mandate. Changes in the policy rate affect monetary and financial conditions. Short- and long-term rates change, and asset prices and the exchange rate move. This affects consumption and investment, as well as imports and exports. According to our estimates for Switzerland, both the 10-year interest rate and the exchange rate go up after a policy rate increase. One year after the increase, both inflation and output are lower. How have we applied our monetary policy strategy? In the years after the global financial crisis, policy rates reached very low levels, both in Switzerland and abroad. Safe-haven flows posed a threat to price stability. In such an environment, it was important to supplement interest rate policy with foreign exchange interventions to safeguard price stability. In 2021, after years of low inflation, inflation started to rise globally. Around the world, supply was constrained, demand was strong and monetary policy was loose. The SNB addressed the resulting inflationary pressure by using a combination of policy rate hikes and foreign-currency sales. This prevented a broadening of inflation and limited second-round effects on domestic prices. Over the past few decades, the SNB has faced many crises that threatened price stability. Despite these repeated challenges, the SNB has fulfilled its mandate - price stability in the medium term.

Funding for research into hydrogen resources
news.body:
Exploratory research work into the commercial viability of hydrogen resources in Southland will be accelerated by a grant of up to $17.8 million from the Regional Infrastructure Fund, Regional Development Minister Shane Jones says.

“This investment is about improving our understanding of hydrogen and whether it can provide New Zealand another source of energy at a time when global access to energy resources is increasingly uncertain,” Mr Jones says.

“Hydrogen presents an exciting economic and emerging energy opportunity. We need to better understand how hydrogen could support New Zealand’s economic growth, strengthen energy security, and build on our natural advantages.

“The research will help establish whether New Zealand’s natural hydrogen resources can be commercially developed. This is an important step towards building a clearer picture of how hydrogen can contribute to our economic prosperity.”

The project, led by Earth Sciences New Zealand in collaboration with University of Canterbury and University of Auckland, is a two-phase early-stage natural and orange hydrogen exploration programme, beginning with a drill site near Bluff in Southland. It will also include investigations into identifying a prospective North Island natural hydrogen drilling location.

“This RIF investment aims to unlock long-term economic value in our regions through the innovative use of New Zealand natural resources,” Mr Jones says.

“The research data from the project is intended to be open access, improving our collective understanding of New Zealand’s natural hydrogen potential and allowing government, researchers and industry to make better-informed decisions about regulation, future exploration, and investment.”

Funding for the project comes from the Government’s $30 million RIF hydrogen package announced in August to help grow the hydrogen sector.

Editors’ note

White hydrogen, also known as natural hydrogen, occurs naturally underground while orange hydrogen is produced through reactions of certain rock formations.

Both are emerging globally as potential lower-emissions sources of hydrogen for industrial processes, fertiliser and chemical production, fuel, and hard-to-electrify sectors such as heavy transport, industry, aviation and the maritime sector.

For more information see: Direction for white and orange hydrogen regulation | Beehive.govt.nz.
